title: Energy demand: buildings, industry, transport
summary: People want services, not energy: warm rooms, steel, passenger-kilometres. See how GCAM grows service demand with income and price, and how transport modes compete on money plus time.
outcomes: You can explain service demand with income and price elasticities
You can compute a mode's generalised cost including the value of time
You can describe GCAM's buildings, industry and transport demand structure
You can trace how the electricity price reaches electric cars and heat pumps
narration_en: Nobody wants a gigajoule for its own sake. People want warm and cool rooms, light, steel for buildings, and trips to work and school. GCAM therefore models demand for energy services first, and only then the fuels needed to deliver them. Service demand grows with income and falls when services get more expensive, through income and price elasticities. Buildings demand depends on floor space, which rises with income and then levels off, and on heating and cooling degree days. Industry is split into sectors such as steel, cement, chemicals and fertiliser. Transport is special because time matters. A trip by bus is cheap in money but slow, while a car or a train is faster. GCAM adds the value of time to the money cost of each mode, using the wage, so as people get richer they move toward faster modes. In this module you will compute service demand, then mode shares for walking, bus, rail and car at three wage levels, and watch the car share grow from three percent to sixty-two percent.
narration_ar: لا أحد يريد جيجاجول من الطاقة لذاته. يريد الناس غرفًا دافئة وباردة، وإضاءة، وفولاذًا للمباني، ورحلات إلى العمل والمدرسة. لذلك يُنمذج GCAM الطلب على خدمات الطاقة أولًا، ثم الوقود اللازم لتقديمها. ينمو الطلب على الخدمات مع الدخل وينخفض عندما ترتفع تكلفتها، عبر مرونات الدخل والسعر. ويعتمد الطلب في المباني على المساحة الأرضية، التي ترتفع مع الدخل ثم تستقر، وعلى أيام التدفئة والتبريد. وتنقسم الصناعة إلى قطاعات مثل الحديد والصلب والإسمنت والكيماويات والأسمدة. أما النقل فحالة خاصة لأن الوقت مهم. فالرحلة بالحافلة رخيصة نقدًا لكنها بطيئة، بينما السيارة أو القطار أسرع. يضيف النموذج قيمة الوقت إلى التكلفة النقدية لكل وسيلة، مستخدمًا الأجر، لذلك ينتقل الناس إلى الوسائل الأسرع كلما زاد ثراؤهم. في هذه الوحدة ستحسب الطلب على الخدمات، ثم حصص المشي والحافلة والقطار والسيارة عند ثلاثة مستويات للأجور، وترى حصة السيارة تنمو من ثلاثة بالمئة إلى اثنين وستين بالمئة.

diagram.title: Energy demand: services first, fuels second
diagram.caption: Income and prices set service demand; technologies then choose fuels. Electricity prices reach every end use.

nodes.label: Income and population
nodes.detail: GDP per person drives floorspace, industrial output and passenger travel through income elasticities (demand_energy.html).

nodes.label: Buildings
nodes.detail: Residential split into 10 income deciles since v7.1. Floorspace follows a Gompertz curve; heating and cooling depend on degree-days (demand_energy.html).

nodes.label: Industry
nodes.detail: Iron and steel, chemicals, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, food processing and other industry, plus construction, mining and agricultural energy use.

nodes.label: Transport
nodes.detail: Four final demands: passenger aviation, other passenger, international shipping, other freight. Nested modes, size classes and drivetrains (Go 3 goes deep).

nodes.label: Value of time
nodes.detail: Passenger mode cost adds W·V/S: wage per hour × time-value multiplier ÷ speed. Faster modes win as wages rise.

nodes.label: Electricity price
nodes.detail: Electric technologies (heat pumps, EVs, electric arc furnaces) pay the solved electricity price, so cheaper power pulls demand toward electricity.

nodes.label: Final energy by fuel
nodes.detail: Technology choice inside each service turns service demand into final energy by fuel.

nodes.label: Emissions
nodes.detail: Combustion CO₂ = fuel use × carbon coefficient; cooling electricity also drives HFC134a (emissions.html).

tour.text: Income per person, from Go 2.1, is the main driver of how much service people demand.
Buildings and industry grow with income and fall with service price; floorspace saturates.
Transport adds the value of time: richer travellers choose faster modes even if dearer.
Inside each service, technologies compete by cost, so electricity prices steer heat pumps and EVs.
Final energy by fuel times carbon coefficients gives demand-side emissions.

sections.heading: Services, not fuels
sections.html:
GCAM's demand sectors produce energy services (floorspace heated and cooled, industrial output, passenger-km and tonne-km), then choose technologies and fuels to supply them (demand_energy.html). Service demand changes with income and price:

Dt = Dt−1 · (Yt/Yt−1)α · (Pt/Pt−1)β · (Nt/Nt−1)

With α = 0.6 and β = −0.3, doubling income raises passenger-km from 100 to 151.6; if travel also becomes 50% dearer it is 134.2.

sections.heading: Buildings
sections.html: Residential demand is split into 10 income deciles (since v7.1). Floorspace per person follows a Gompertz curve in income and population density; services per m² saturate; heating and cooling scale with degree-days and shell efficiency (demand_energy.html). Degree-days link buildings to climate; the helios tool computes them from gridded data. Parameter values for these curves are not given on the doc pages.

sections.heading: Industry
sections.html: Industry includes iron and steel (BOF, EAF with scrap, EAF with DRI), chemicals, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, food processing and other industry, plus construction, mining and agricultural energy. Fertiliser demand is the sum of crop production × fertiliser coefficient: a direct link from farms to the energy system (demand_energy.html).

sections.heading: Transport: money plus time
sections.html:
Each vehicle technology has a cost per passenger-km or tonne-km:

Pj = (Pfuel · Ij + Nj) / Lj

with fuel intensity I, non-fuel cost per vehicle-km N and load factor L. Passenger modes then add the value of time:

Pmode = Σ αj Pj + W · V / S

W is wage per hour (GDP per person ÷ working hours), V a time-value multiplier, S speed. In the kit toy (value of time = half the wage), car share rises from 3% at $2/h to 22.5% at $10/h and 61.7% at $40/h.

callouts.title: A useful mental model
callouts.html: A restaurant plans meals before it orders gas. GCAM does the same: meals = services, gas = fuels. Change the menu (services) or the stove (technology) and the gas bill changes.

callouts.title: In GCAM
callouts.html: Query final energy consumption by sector and fuel and transport service output by mode (outputs_quantity.html). Transport inputs are built by gcamdata from the UCD transportation database (UCD_trn_data_SSP*.csv) (ssp.html). Note: transport units changed in v8.5 (billion pkm, 1975$); Go 3.2 covers the details.

callouts.title: "Richer people always drive more"
callouts.html: Not necessarily: they choose faster modes. Where high-speed rail is fast and frequent, rising wages can favour rail. The value of time rewards speed, not cars as such.

explorer.intro: Change the wage, speeds and money costs, and watch the generalised cost and mode shares.
explorer.predict: If wages quadruple from $10 to $40 an hour, does the bus share rise or fall? By roughly how much?

code.title: Service demand and mode choice with time cost
code.explain: Service demand with elasticities, then mode shares from money cost + value of time at three wages. Try: double rail speed and predict the new rail share at $40/h.

takeaways: GCAM models energy services first, then the fuels that supply them
Service demand rises with income (α) and falls with price (β)
Buildings use floorspace and degree-days; industry is split into subsectors
Passenger modes compete on money cost plus wage-based time cost
The electricity price reaches heat pumps, EVs and electric furnaces through technology choice

quiz.q: Income doubles, α = 0.6, price unchanged. Service demand rises by a factor of…
In GCAM's passenger cost, W·V/S represents…
Why do faster modes gain share as wages rise?
quiz.explain: The time term grows with the wage and is smaller for fast modes.
